vignette: Declan had never imagined the basement of his old duplex would become a place he couldn’t enter without his pulse jumping to his throat. The night it happened began with a snapped pilot light on their water heater and a rushed match. He remembered the sharp flare, the heat catching his flannel sleeve, and the sudden lurch of his partner’s hand grabbing his collar. What started as a muffled argument over bills fractured into shoving, then a heavy fall onto concrete, followed by his shoulder cracking against a cast-iron pipe. The air filled with the acrid sting of scorched fabric and hot metal. When it ended, Declan dragged himself out, leaving the door unlocked as if running faster than his legs could carry him. He told himself it was a one-time failure of temper, something to be managed. But the basement door stayed shut, and he stopped going down to the utility room, telling himself the old water heater was leaking anyway. The changes did not arrive as sudden breaks but as quiet recalibrations. At work, Declan could feel his jaw tighten the moment a homeowner’s voice rose in complaint about a delayed estimate. He had come to believe that even a measured, quiet expression of frustration carried the same invisible charge as the night in the basement. He began leaving jobs early when disputes flared over pipe replacements, telling his foreman he had a family emergency. At home, the olfactory world became a minefield. A neighbor’s charcoal grill drifting through an open window, the faint tang of burnt toast, even the scent of a welding torch on his truck caught his breath and sent his hands trembling to his keys. He was certain the air itself had turned hostile, that waiting in the smell any longer would let the past walk back through the door. Sometimes the memory arrived not as a narrative but as a sudden heaviness in his ribs, a phantom pressure against his collarbone that made the kitchen tiles feel like concrete. He actively sidestepped thinking about the event, rerouting his attention the moment it surfaced, refusing to trace the edges of it. He stayed awake until three in the morning, scrolling through repair manuals or watching old games, convinced that sleep was a trap where the floor would catch him. He avoided the site of the basement entirely, taking long detours through neighborhood streets just to keep it out of his line of sight. When his wife tried to speak with him about the distance growing between them, he changed the subject or stepped outside, certain that any attempt to untangle the past would only prove him unworthy of the life they had built. The habits accumulated without ceremony: he stopped taking residential calls in certain zip codes, began eating lunch alone to avoid conversation, and stopped mentioning the days his chest tightened at the sound of a dropped wrench. By the time Declan walked into the clinic, the calendar had already turned twice. He carried a worn leather satchel of pressure gauges, his boots still dusted with drywall. What finally brought him through the door was not a breaking point but a quiet exhaustion; he had noticed his wife weeping silently in the kitchen while he sat at his bed’s edge, refusing to ask why, afraid that asking would only teach her how to flinch at his voice. He wanted to stop checking the locks three times, wanted to walk past a grilling neighbor without scanning for an exit, and wanted to sleep through the night without counting the minutes until dawn.
